title: Old age
hookLine: honoring the old: Confucius waits for the elders with staffs, and the Torah says rise
tomorrow: an old man, nearly blind, crossed his hands to bless. why?

lines: THE BEST CHAIR, THE FIRST PLATE.
cards: At some weddings, the oldest aunt gets the best chair and the first plate, and nobody has to say why. Confucius would have noticed. The Analects keep a small scene from his village.
When the villagers were drinking together, he didn't leave whenever he felt like it. He waited. When the old people with their walking staffs went out, then he went out, right after them.
The book records no speech about it, only the detail, kept by students who were watching.

teach.b: So, today's question: what's owed to the old? Confucius's answer starts with a word, xiao, usually translated filial piety: the reverence children owe their parents.
Its partner, ti, is the respect the young owe their elders. He's blunt about what it isn't. A student asks him about it, and he says: these days it means feeding your parents.

teach.h: DOGS AND HORSES GET FED TOO.
teach.b: But dogs and horses get fed too. Without reverence, what's the difference? Another student asks, and he says the hard part is the face: doing the chores isn't enough if you do them with a sour look.
So honor, for Confucius, lives in the body and the manner. You wait, you mind your face, you let the old go first, and you mean it. Even leaving a party was a lesson.
Here's a neighbor who says something close.
The Torah: "Thou shalt rise up before the hoary head, and honour the face of the old man, and fear thy God: I am the LORD." Shared: honor you can see. Stand up.
Look them in the face. And one honest difference.

For Confucius, the root is the family and the rites of the village; reverence for elders grows out of reverence for your own parents. Leviticus ties it straight to God, and to every gray head, kin or stranger.
Both put honor where it can be seen.

how: Confucian tradition calls reverence for parents xiao, filial piety, and pairs it with ti, respect for elders, both shown in manner as well as support. The Torah commands rising before the aged (Leviticus 19:32), and some Jews still stand when an elder enters the room.

o: the age when you can stop working for good
a medical word for the slowing of the body
honor for the old, shown in how you wait and rise

games.q: honoring the old: tap the pairs.
p: waited for the elders with staffs
get fed too: what's missing is reverence
rise up before the hoary head

s: for Confucius, supporting your parents with food and money is enough
he says dogs and horses are fed too; without reverence, what's the difference?
the Torah tells people to rise before the old
Leviticus 19:32: rise up before the hoary head, and honor the face of the old man.
Confucius and Leviticus root honor for the old in exactly the same thing
Confucius roots it in family and village rites; Leviticus ties it to God, and to every gray head.

games.q: at a family dinner, your teen cousin serves grandpa his plate while scrolling and sighing. "i did the chore." what would Confucius say?
o: the chore isn't enough; the hard part is the face, doing it with reverence.
he's done his duty; feeding an elder is all that filial piety means.
he should skip it; reverence only counts if he feels it first.
games.why: asked about filial piety, Confucius said the difficulty is the countenance. Feeding without reverence is how dogs and horses are kept.

practice: Bring to mind one elder you haven't seen in a while: a grandparent, a neighbor, an old teacher. Picture them walking into the room, and sit up a little taller, as if you'd just risen for them.
Choose one question you'd ask about their life when you next visit. Then sit quietly with their face in mind for the rest of the time.

wordCard.voice: Old age: in Confucius's teaching, honor for parents and elders shown in the body, waiting until the elders with staffs have gone out.

orig.note: Chinese: xiao, filial piety; the reverence owed to parents.

carryVoice: Your line: honor the old. Rise before the gray head, and wait for the staffs to go first. See you tomorrow.

sources.ref: Analects 10.10 (Legge's numbering: when the villagers were drinking together, on those who carried staffs going out, he went out immediately after)
Analects 2.7 (Ziyou asks about filial piety: dogs and horses are also supported; without reverence, what is the difference?) and 2.8 (Zixia asks: the difficulty is with the countenance)
